scope: The connected Toitū Otago Settlers Museum in Dunedin, with the Edwardian Burnside galleries, rounded Art Deco rail depot, rear collections ranges and modern glazed Josephine Foyer.

references.caption: Josephine, a double-ended Robert Fairlie-designed locomotive, was one of two locomotives used in 1872 on the newly-completed Dunedin – Port Chalmers Railway. After about 25 years service in Otago and in the Wanganui district, Josephine was taken over by the Public Works Department for use in railway construction at various locations including sections of the Otago Central, North Island Main trunk, and Midland lines. In 1917 Josephine was sold to the Otago Iron Rolling Mills Co. as scrap but no one was keen to demolish the old engine and when one of the company’s boilers failed Josephine was recommissioned as a temporary steam supply. In 1925 Josephine was installed as an exhibit at the New Zealand and South Seas International Exhibition in Dunedin and afterwards was presented to the Otago Early Settlers Association. In the 1960s

originalReview.notes: The original CC0 foyer photograph shows full-height transparent glazing, widely spaced black square posts and thin transoms. Geometry only; exclude signage, contents and incidental surroundings.

The period printed postcard depicts the original Burnside facade, including the pilaster bays, raised stone plinth, cornice, balustrades and the two pedimented round-arched doorways. The publisher’s initials appear on the recto and the price and printer imprint establish the published postcard. Modern wings are outside this view.

quallaSearch.notes: Qualla first. The exact native CC0 Spragg foyer photograph shows the glazing and supports. The only Qualla museum exterior labeled public domain has unresolved authorship in its original attribution, so it was excluded. The supplemental printed postcard is dated 1904–1915 in Te Papa’s native catalogue. Both sides were inspected. No attribution-only images were used.
